name: French Blue
lede: French Blue is a strong blue with three histories: the blue of France's royal arms and flag, a name for artificial ultramarine, and a famous stolen diamond.

sections.title: The blue of France
sections.body:
Pastoureau treats the royal azure of France, a field of gold fleurs-de-lis on blue, as a continuous French blue since the twelfth century [1]. In the thirteenth century that azure became the color of the monarchy, and in the late Middle Ages the color of royal officers [1]. After 1789 the tricolor cockade carried the blue into the Revolution and then the national flag [1].

The swatch here is the modern screen color, a strong blue in the ISCC-NBS system (block 194), about 3.1 units from it [2]. It is not a measured heraldic blue [2][1].

sections.title: French blue as ultramarine
sections.body:
In the pigment trade French blue was a synonym for synthetic ultramarine, specifically French ultramarine [3]. Salter in 1869 described a middle shade, new blue, between French blue and permanent blue [4]. The term appears in the long list of ultramarine names with Guimet's blue, laundry blue and permanent mauve [5].

In the same lists, Prussian blue also carried the label French blue among its many trade names, which shows how loosely the term was used [6]. Livingstone shows that the modern pigment Ultramarine French Blue looks like a pure blue, though the cobalt blue next to it reflects into the green [7].

sections.title: The French Blue diamond
sections.body: A different French blue is a gem [8]. The French Blue diamond was stolen in a famous robbery and never seen again as such [8]. About twenty years later a slightly different blue diamond appeared in London, the second-largest fancy blue recorded up to then [8]. In 2005 the Smithsonian's Jeffrey Post commissioned a cubic zirconia cut in the shape of the French Blue and had it recut in the shape of the Hope [8].

sections.title: In the color lists
sections.body: Paterson lists French blue among the blues alongside French navy, which is a shade of navy, and French green, French grey and others [9]. The term was a general label for a French-made or French-fashion blue, and no single standard shade is given [9]. Close relatives are [[cobalt]], [[royal-blue]] and [[azure]], which are all strong mid blues [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color near this swatch appears in 11 works, or 0.05 per cent, rarer than 77 per cent of the named colors [10]. Nine paintings hold it on at least 5 per cent of the canvas, among them Van Gogh's *Two Poplars in the Alpilles* of 1889 and, the earliest, Fra Angelico's *Madonna of the Pomegranate* of 1426 [10]. As always these are photographs of varnished paintings [10].
